blocks.text: General physical examination in pregnancy is a systematic assessment of the pregnant woman to determine her general health, identify pre-existing medical conditions, detect pregnancy-related complications and assess her physiological adaptation to pregnancy.
It is an essential component of:
Assessment of pregnant women presenting with complaints.
The examination should assess both normal physiological changes associated with pregnancy and abnormal findings that may indicate underlying disease.
Assess the general wellbeing of the pregnant woman.
Detect anaemia, jaundice, cyanosis and nutritional deficiencies.
Identify thyroid disease and other endocrine abnormalities.
Assess the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.
Identify evidence of infection or systemic disease.
Establish baseline clinical parameters for subsequent antenatal visits.
A complete initial assessment includes vital signs, general examination and relevant systemic examinations. Some components are repeated at subsequent antenatal visits depending on clinical need.
Greet the patient and introduce yourself.
Explain the examination and obtain informed consent.
Ask whether she has any pain, breathlessness, dizziness or other discomfort.
Ask permission before exposing any part of the body.
Position her comfortably, initially sitting upright where appropriate.
Avoid prolonged supine positioning, particularly in advanced pregnancy, because the gravid uterus may compress the inferior vena cava and cause supine hypotensive symptoms.
If she becomes dizzy or hypotensive while supine, turn her onto her left side.
Important OSCE point: Always maintain dignity, explain each manoeuvre and obtain consent before examination.
Begin by standing at the end of the examination couch and observing the patient.

blocks.text: A new BP of at least 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive woman raises concern for gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
Pre-eclampsia is hypertension after 20 weeks accompanied by proteinuria and/or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction, depending on the diagnostic criteria used.

subsections.subsection_title: How to present your findings to an examiner (OSCE)

blocks.text: After completing the examination, summarise your findings systematically.
Example of a normal examination presentation:
"The patient is a pregnant woman who is conscious, alert and comfortable at rest. She is well nourished and not in obvious respiratory distress.
There is no obvious pallor, jaundice, cyanosis or facial puffiness. There is no significant peripheral lymphadenopathy or thyroid enlargement.
Her vital signs are as follows: blood pressure ___ mmHg, pulse rate ___ beats per minute, respiratory rate ___ breaths per minute, temperature ___ °C and oxygen saturation ___%.
There is no significant pedal or sacral oedema.
Cardiovascular examination reveals normal heart sounds without pathological murmurs. Respiratory examination reveals normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without added sounds.
There are no obvious abnormalities on the other components of the general physical examination.
In summary, this is a pregnant woman who is clinically stable, with no significant abnormality detected on general physical examination."
If abnormalities are present: State them explicitly and explain their clinical significance. Never describe a patient as normal when you have identified an abnormal finding.
